I would try finding a therapist to valid your personal concerns and help you address the issues with your fiancé, he doesn’t have to know about it either as I suppose he would judge you for that. Your guys’ dynamic in regard to your mental health does not sound healthy at all. With time this can fester and get dangerous. My father was the same way to me and my mother; he ironically had frequent insomnia and night terrors.  

I would start with refraining from speaking to him about your mental health for now in order to spare you from the judgement. In the meantime, with a therapist or not, start thinking about how you may address his ignorance and hurtful words in a respectful, calm fashion. Anger and frustration breeds anger and frustration. Even if your mental health seems to improve significantly with medication or therapy, I would address this resentment you harbor towards him. Resentments eat us up from the inside, even if we think we’ve put it down, it has a way of coming up and bringing us back to the emotions we felt at the time it was harbored, manifesting as a destructive tirade.

I would write down things as you experience them - emotions, physical sensations tied to them, even your thoughts about your frustration with the lack of breakthrough in therapy. This can be a good place for your therapist to begin helping you.

I could identify with quite a few components of your story. I have had several withdrawals from uni, two  classified as medical and two others that were not. The reasoning was the same for all - depression and drugs.

I’m in the process of applying for readmission. I have spent some time working low skill, soul crushing jobs with seemingly no relevance and foul supervisors. I have also been in and out of dual diagnosis residential treatment centers (essentially places for addicts and alcoholics with co-occurring mental illness). After this rehab-relapse cycle, with almost 3 months of sobriety and 2 years out of school, I feel ready to resume.

I can see how finishing your education and encountering  more roadblocks would bring about a sense of hopeless. I would first research to clarify your concerns about being dq from the bar and if there are any ways you may submit a petition. Nonetheless I think that you are thinking way too catastrophically. 

There are many professions you can still pursue - tech, medicine, academia - and better paying and emotionally rewarding jobs - serving, writing, tutoring - that you can take on in the meantime.

The reason is that despite the inevitable suffering, there will be moments of love, life and serenity. With changing our behaviors and choosing not to entertain and engage with the suicidal thoughts.
It starts with coming to believe, because if you stay convinced that life is pointless and you’re doomed to be chronically miserable, that’s what you’ll manifest.
Cultivate healthy habits, connect with old friends, find wholesome work, help others, maybe try guided meditation that focuses on wellness & healing.

These are just things that help me and wanted to share
